blogTitle: How to Choose a LIMS: The Evaluation Checklist for Regulated Labs (+ Scorecard)
elevenlabsPodcastSourceText:
This is the podcast brief from Confident LIMS, generated with AI voice narration. Today: how to choose a LIMS, a Laboratory Information Management System, without getting sold one.

Most LIMS evaluations go sideways in the first week. Not because the buyer picks the wrong vendor, but because they start by comparing features instead of deciding what their lab actually needs. Feature lists are written by vendors. Your requirements aren't.

Point one. Start with a one-page requirements brief. Cover your lab's size and number of sites, the regulatory environment you operate in, your sample types and turnaround commitments, and the systems the LIMS has to talk to. Split it into user, system, and functional requirements. Every demo gets measured against that one page.

Point two. Score every vendor on the same seven categories: industry fit, configurability, compliance coverage, integration, user experience, support and time-to-value, and cost transparency. Weight each one before the demos, while you're still objective. Essential is worth eight points, Preferred four, Optional two. Score each vendor zero to five, multiply, and keep it to no more than four Essentials. If everything is essential, nothing is.

Point three. Know the difference between configurable and customizable. Configurable means your team changes workflows, fields, and templates through the interface, with no code. Customizable means a developer writes code against your instance, and you revalidate that code every time the platform updates. That one question predicts your three-year cost better than the price sheet does.

Point four. End every demo with the most useful question on the list: what does your product not do well? Every honest vendor has an answer. Here's ours. If your lab needs deeply bespoke, code-level modifications, a customizable platform with a developer team attached will fit you better than we will. We're configurable by design, and that's a trade-off, not a superpower.

The full checklist, the weighted scorecard, and all eight demo questions are on the Confident LIMS blog at confident lims dot com. Thanks for listening.

How to Choose a LIMS: The Evaluation Checklist for Regulated Labs, plus a Scorecard.
Most LIMS evaluations go sideways in the first week. Not because the buyer picks the wrong vendor — because they start by comparing features instead of deciding what their lab actually needs. Feature lists are written by vendors. Yours aren't.

So, how do you choose a LIMS — a Laboratory Information Management System?
Choose a LIMS by writing a one-page requirements brief first, then scoring every vendor against the same weighted criteria: industry fit, configurability, compliance coverage, integration, user experience, support and time-to-value, and cost transparency. Weight each criterion Essential, Preferred, or Optional before you sit through a demo. The system with the highest weighted score wins — not the vendor with the best presenter.
Start with a requirements brief, not a feature list.
Before you look at a single screenshot, answer one question: what business problem are we solving?
Write the answer down on one page. It should cover your lab's size and number of sites, the regulatory environment you operate in — I-S-O seventeen-oh-twenty-five, NEE-lap and T-N-I, twenty-one C-F-R Part Eleven, Metrc or BioTrack, F-S-M-A — your sample types and turnaround commitments, and the systems this has to talk to: instruments, accounting, C-R-M.
Then split those requirements into three buckets, because vendors will happily blur them.
User requirements — what a person in your lab needs to do. An analyst logs forty samples in under ten minutes.
System requirements — the environment it has to run in. Cloud, single sign-on, data residency, retention.
Functional requirements — what the software must produce. A Certificate of Analysis, or COA, with your accreditation body's required fields on it.
That one page becomes your internal source of truth. Every demo gets measured against it, and when two people on your team disagree about a vendor, you'll find the disagreement is usually about the brief, not the software.
The seven categories that actually decide the outcome.
One. Industry fit.
A LIMS built for your lab type saves you months. A cannabis lab in New York needs Metrc reporting and automatic flagging when a result crosses an action limit. An environmental lab needs method-level Q-C, batch structures, and reporting that a T-N-I assessor recognizes on sight. A food lab needs allergen and pathogen workflows with traceability that survives an F-S-M-A two-oh-four request.
Ask vendors to show you their configuration for your industry, live. Not a slide about it.
Two. Configurability.
Can your team change a workflow, add a field, or adjust a report template without filing a ticket?
This is the single criterion with the longest financial tail, and it gets its own section shortly. For now: look for no-code workflow changes, permission controls your Q-A manager can administer, and a template library you can start from.
Three. Compliance coverage.
No vendor is "twenty-one C-F-R Part Eleven certified." There is no such certificate. What a LIMS can do is help you comply — through audit trails, electronic signatures, versioned records, and access controls that your own validation demonstrates.
So ask for the artifacts: validation documentation, I-Q, O-Q, P-Q protocols, and a live walkthrough of the audit log with a record being changed in front of you. If those only appear after you sign, that tells you what you need to know.
Four. Integration.
Your LIMS sits in the middle of a stack. Ask specifically: Which instruments are already connected — H-P-L-C, GC mass spec, I-C-P mass spec, balances — and how does the data arrive? Does it report to Metrc, BioTrack, or your state's system without a manual export? Is there a documented A-P-I, and can you see it?
"We can integrate with anything" is not an answer. Ask what's already built.
Five. User experience.
Your analysts will use this system every hour of every shift. Count the clicks to log a sample during the demo. Ask whether a bench tech can work from a tablet next to the instrument. Ask how a client retrieves a COA.
A system your team quietly avoids is a system you paid for twice.
Six. Support and time-to-value.
Support consistently ranks at or near the top of what lab buyers say they care about — and it's the criterion most scorecards underweight. Ask for the actual commitments: response time, resolution time, whether onboarding is measured in weeks or quarters, and who owns your migration.
Confident's numbers here are fast onboarding, same-day support response, and one-to-two-day resolution. Ask every vendor on your list for the equivalent, in writing.
Seven. Cost transparency.
You're scoring the three-year cost, not the first invoice. Ask what's included and what isn't: implementation, data migration, additional users, sandbox environments, A-P-I access, report templates, and what an upgrade costs. If pricing is "custom quote only" with nothing published, you'll spend the evaluation negotiating instead of comparing.
The weighted scorecard: Essential eight, Preferred four, Optional two.
Here's the part most buying guides skip. Weight the criteria before the demos, while you're still objective.
Give each line one of three weights. Essential — eight points. Without it, the lab can't operate or can't pass an audit. Preferred — four points. Real value, but you'd survive a workaround. Optional — two points. Nice to have.
Then score each vendor zero to five on how well they meet it, and multiply. Same scale, same scorer, every vendor.

Compliance coverage: audit trail, e-signatures, validation documentation, and I-Q, O-Q, P-Q — typically Essential. Integration: instruments, state reporting, and a documented A-P-I — Essential or Preferred depending on your stack. User experience: clicks per sample, bench usability, client COA retrieval — typically Preferred. Support and time-to-value: response and resolution commitments, onboarding duration, and migration ownership — typically Essential. Cost transparency: three-year total, published inclusions, and upgrade cost — typically Preferred.
Two rules keep this honest. First, no more than four Essentials — if everything is essential, nothing is. Second, score from what you saw in the demo, not from the proposal.
Configurable versus customizable: the question that predicts your three-year cost.
These two words get used interchangeably in sales calls. They describe opposite futures.
Configurable means your team changes workflows, fields, templates, and permissions themselves, through the interface, with no code. The change takes an afternoon. It survives the next upgrade.

Ask the question directly: when our Q-A manager needs a new field on the COA next quarter, who does the work, how long does it take, and what does it cost? The answer predicts your third-year invoice better than the price sheet does.
Demo questions that expose a weak vendor.
Bring these to every demo. Ask them in the same order, and write down the answers.
Step one. Show me a sample logged, tested, and released to a client — end to end, in my industry's configuration.

Step five. What's your onboarding timeline, and what does your team do versus what mine does?

An environmental lab needs method-level QC, batch structures, and reporting that a TNI assessor recognizes on sight. Support consistently ranks at or near the top of what lab buyers say they care about — and it's the criterion most scorecards underweight. Ask for the actual commitments: response time, resolution time, whether onboarding is measured in weeks or quarters, and who owns your migration.

You're scoring the three-year cost, not the first invoice. Ask what's included and what isn't: implementation, data migration, additional users, sandbox environments, API access, report templates, and what an upgrade costs. The weighted scorecard: Essential 8, Preferred 4, Optional 2

Here's the part most buying guides skip. Weight the criteria before the demos, while you're still objective.

Give each line one of three weights:

  • Essential — 8 points. Without it, the lab can't operate or can't pass an audit.

  • Optional — 2 points. Nice to have.

  • Industry fit — Your industry's workflows and reporting, configured and shown live. Typical weight: Essential.
  • Configurability — No-code changes your team makes without the vendor. Typical weight: Essential.
  • Compliance coverage — Audit trail, e-signatures, validation documentation, IQ/OQ/PQ. Typical weight: Essential.
  • Integration — Instruments, state reporting, documented API. Typical weight: Essential or Preferred.
  • User experience — Clicks per sample, bench usability, client COA retrieval. Typical weight: Preferred.
